# Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready {#sec-windows}

This appendix is step 1 of the setup (@sec-step-ready) for Windows. The workshop's tools are made for
Linux, so on Windows you install **Ubuntu**, a widely used version of Linux, inside Windows with **WSL**,
the Windows Subsystem for Linux. Think of Windows as your house, with your browser, files and apps, and
Ubuntu as a room inside it, a window where you type commands. Everything in this book happens in that room,
your Windows browser still opens what you make, and nothing on Windows is removed.

Why not PowerShell, Windows's own command window? Because the book's commands, and the way the setup was
tested, are for Linux. Some tools have Windows installers, but their paths and commands differ, and each
variant is another way to go wrong.

@fig-windows-session shows the whole procedure in one window. The steps below go slowly, with a restart in
the middle, and the first time Ubuntu opens it also asks you to choose a username and password, which the
animation skips.

![The whole procedure in one PowerShell window: install, check, `wsl` starts Ubuntu, and `whoami` prints your name. An illustration drawn for the workshop.](../media/gifs/windows-session.gif){#fig-windows-session .anim fig-alt="An animated PowerShell window. Five commands run one after another: wsl --install -d Ubuntu --no-launch prints that Ubuntu has been installed; wsl -l -v lists Ubuntu with VERSION 2; wsl starts Ubuntu, and the prompt changes from PS C:\Users\ana> to ana@LAPTOP:~$; whoami prints ana; exit returns to the PowerShell prompt."}

## Before you start {.unnumbered}

- About **20 minutes** and **one restart**.
- An **administrator account** on this computer. On a work laptop, ask IT first; if IT types the password
  for you, stay signed in as yourself. Without one, WSL cannot be installed: arrange to work with someone
  else's computer.
- **Windows 11**, or Windows 10 version 2004 or newer (Settings → System → About shows yours).
- Plugged in, on a strong connection: Ubuntu is a big download.
- These instructions on a second screen or a phone, because the restart closes your browser.

Do one step, compare your screen with **You should see**, then go on. If something looks different, see
[If you are stuck](#sec-windows-stuck).

## Step 1: open PowerShell as administrator {.unnumbered #sec-win-1}

PowerShell is a Windows window for typing commands; you need it for a few minutes only.

1. Press the **Windows key**, or click the Windows logo on the taskbar, and type `PowerShell`.
2. **Right-click** "Windows PowerShell" and choose **Run as administrator**.
3. Choose **Yes** when Windows asks.

![Searching for PowerShell from the Start button. A drawing of Windows 11; on Windows 10 the button sits at the left, and the steps are the same.](../media/deck/windows-steps/start-search){width=70% fig-alt="A drawing of the Windows desktop. The Start button, the four-square Windows logo in the middle of the bottom taskbar, is circled. Above it the search panel has PowerShell typed in and Windows PowerShell as the best match."}

![The right-click menu, with Run as administrator circled.](../media/deck/windows-steps/run-as-admin){width=70% fig-alt="A drawing of the Windows PowerShell search result with a right-click menu open. Run as administrator is highlighted and circled."}

::: {.callout-note title="You should see"}
A window whose title starts with "Administrator", ending in a line like `PS C:\WINDOWS\system32>`.

![The administrator window.](../media/deck/windows-steps/admin-window){width=70% fig-alt="A drawing of a dark blue PowerShell window. Its title bar reads Administrator: Windows PowerShell, circled. The last line is the prompt PS C:\WINDOWS\system32 followed by a greater-than sign."}
:::

## Step 2: turn on WSL {.unnumbered #sec-win-2}

Paste this into the PowerShell window (Ctrl+V, or a right-click if that does nothing) and press **Enter**:

```powershell
wsl --install -d Ubuntu --no-launch
```

::: transcript
```text
PS C:\WINDOWS\system32> wsl --install -d Ubuntu --no-launch
Installing: Virtual Machine Platform
Virtual Machine Platform has been installed.
Installing: Windows Subsystem for Linux
Windows Subsystem for Linux has been installed.
Installing: Ubuntu
Ubuntu has been installed.
The requested operation is successful. Changes will not be effective until the system is rebooted.
```
:::

::: {.callout-note title="You should see"}
A message that you must restart, such as "Changes will not be effective until the system is rebooted". If
instead it says Ubuntu is installed or "already exists", skip to step 5.
:::

## Step 3: restart the computer {.unnumbered #sec-win-3}

Save your work, then Start → Power → **Restart**.

::: why
The command runs twice because, when a restart is needed, the first run only turns on Windows features and
installs no Linux at all (checked against WSL's source code, version 3.0.3, on 2026-11-06). `--no-launch`
keeps Ubuntu's first start out of the administrator window, whose folder is a Windows system folder.
:::

## Step 4: download Ubuntu {.unnumbered #sec-win-4}

1. Open a **normal** PowerShell window, not as administrator: press the Windows key, type `PowerShell`, and
   press Enter. Ubuntu is installed for the account that runs this line, so it must be yours.
2. Paste the **same line** and press Enter:

```powershell
wsl --install -d Ubuntu --no-launch
```

This is the long wait: the download can take many minutes, and the percentage may stand still for a while.

::: {.callout-note title="You should see"}
That it finished, or "already exists". Both mean go on. Keep this window open.
:::

You will now have two windows, and their last line tells them apart: PowerShell's ends in `>` (like
`PS C:\Users\Ana>`), Ubuntu's in `$` (like `ana@LAPTOP:~$`). PowerShell is only for steps 1, 2, 4 and 6;
everything else happens in Ubuntu.

## Step 5: open Ubuntu, and choose a username and password {.unnumbered #sec-win-5}

1. Press the **Windows key**, type `Ubuntu`, and press **Enter**. The first start unpacks files: wait.
2. **Username:** one short word in lower case, with no spaces, such as `ana`. It need not match your Windows
   name.
3. **Password:** type one you will remember, press Enter, and type it again.

::: pitfall
Nothing appears while you type the password: no dots, no stars. That is normal; keep typing and press Enter.
Write the password down: `sudo` asks for it in step 8.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="You should see"}
A *prompt*, the line that means "ready for a command", with your own names: `ana@LAPTOP:~$`. `ana` is you,
`LAPTOP` this computer, `~` your home folder, and `$` where you type. In this Ubuntu window, type `whoami`
and press Enter: it prints your username.
:::

## Step 6: check that Ubuntu runs on WSL 2 {.unnumbered #sec-win-6}

In the **PowerShell** window (its line ends in `>`):

```powershell
wsl -l -v
```

::: {.callout-note title="You should see"}
Ubuntu with a **2** in the VERSION column:

```text
  NAME      STATE           VERSION
* Ubuntu    Running         2
```
:::

If it says **1**, run `wsl --set-version Ubuntu 2` and wait. Then type `exit` to close PowerShell.

## Step 7: practise copy and paste {.unnumbered #sec-win-7}

| | With the mouse | With the keyboard |
|---|---|---|
| **Copy** | select the text, then right-click | select the text, then **Ctrl+Shift+C** |
| **Paste** | right-click with nothing selected | **Ctrl+Shift+V** |

: Copy and paste in Windows Terminal. The keyboard way does nothing in some older windows; the mouse always works. {#tbl-win-copy}

::: pitfall
**Ctrl+C** with nothing selected does not copy: it *stops* whatever is running. If that happens, run the
command again.
:::

Copy `echo "Paste works"`, paste it into Ubuntu and press Enter; the next line should say `Paste works`.

## Step 8: install two small tools {.unnumbered #sec-win-8}

```bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl git
```

`sudo` means "do this as administrator" and asks for your Ubuntu password from step 5, hidden again; `apt`
is Ubuntu's installer; `&&` means "and then, if that worked". A lot of text scrolls past. When the `$` comes
back, check:

```bash
curl --version && git --version
```

::: {.callout-note title="You should see"}
A version number for each, such as `git version 2.43.0`. Yours may differ.
:::

## Step 9: four habits {.unnumbered #sec-win-9}

**Stay in your home folder.** Keep project folders there, not in Documents, Desktop or OneDrive. If the
prompt shows `/mnt/c`, you are in a Windows folder: `cd ~` goes home. (Windows drives appear under `/mnt/`;
keeping projects in `~` is also faster.)

**See your files in Windows.** `explorer.exe .` opens the current folder in File Explorer, where you can
double-click what you made.

**Open a second tab.** Ctrl+Shift+D duplicates the tab; you will need one while the assistant is busy in the
first. A new tab may start in the home folder, so `cd` back into your project.

**Copy sign-in links whole.** Ubuntu may not be able to open your browser, so tools print a link: copy all of
it into your Windows browser, and if the website shows a code, paste it back into Ubuntu.

::: pitfall
Don't install the Windows versions of Quarto, Python or a coding assistant for this book. Ubuntu needs its own
copies, and the Windows ones can get in the way.
:::

Step 1 is done when `wsl -l -v` shows Ubuntu with VERSION 2, an Ubuntu window shows a prompt ending in `$`,
`git --version` prints a version in Ubuntu, and you know your Ubuntu password. Continue with @sec-step-terminal.
Next time, open Ubuntu from the Start menu: your files are still there.

## Useful PowerShell commands {.unnumbered #sec-win-commands}

| Command (in PowerShell) | Does |
|---|---|
| `wsl -l -v` | lists each Linux with its state and WSL version (from Ubuntu: `wsl.exe -l -v`) |
| `wsl --user root` | opens a root shell, the documented way to reset a forgotten password with `passwd <username>` |
| `wsl --shutdown` | stops every running Linux at once, including the assistant and any preview: save your work first |

: Three WSL commands worth knowing (Microsoft's WSL documentation, checked 2026-10-31). {#tbl-wsl-commands}

## If you are stuck {.unnumbered #sec-windows-stuck}

| You see | Do this |
|---|---|
| The install stuck at 0.0% | Close it, then in PowerShell run `wsl --install --web-download --no-launch -d Ubuntu` |
| No Ubuntu in the Start menu | Do step 4 again in a normal window, not as administrator; still none? In PowerShell type `wsl ~` |
| Error `0x80370102`, or "virtualization is not enabled" | Virtualization is off in the computer's BIOS; without BIOS access this cannot be fixed |
| A list of options and no install | Windows is too old: run Windows Update, restart, repeat step 2 |
| "Access denied", or no Run as administrator | You need an administrator account |
| "Already exists" | Ubuntu is installed: go to step 5 |
| `wsl` is "not found" | You are in Ubuntu: use PowerShell, whose line ends in `>` |
| Ubuntu closes or won't start | Restart the computer and open Ubuntu again |

: What to do when installing goes wrong (steps 1 to 5). {#tbl-windows-stuck}

| You see | Do this |
|---|---|
| Nothing moves, and the title starts with "Select" | A click paused the window: press Esc |
| A download fails on a work network | Try another network, such as a phone hotspot |
| The prompt starts with `root@` and ends in `#` | The username step was skipped: ask for help before going on |
| `sudo` says "Sorry, try again" | Wrong password: type it again slowly, it stays hidden |
| Forgotten Ubuntu password | In PowerShell, `wsl -u root`, then `passwd ana` with your username, then `exit` |
| `command not found` right after an install | Open a new tab or window and try again |

: What to do when Ubuntu runs but a step goes wrong. {#tbl-windows-stuck-ubuntu}

For anything else, copy the command and the full error into a web chat, say "Windows, Ubuntu on WSL", and
try one suggested fix at a time, never pasting a password.

These steps were written from Microsoft's WSL documentation (install, setup, basic commands, file systems
and troubleshooting, checked 2026-11-06) and have been checked on a Mac against that documentation, not yet
on a clean Windows machine. Exact messages can differ between Windows versions.
